description: We are a team of engineering students with great interest in the challenges proposed by NASA in this hackathon. We are hoping to learn, collaborate, and grow our skills so we can make an impact.
summary: ShackleComm is an interactive web application for exploring the lighting and communication conditions at candidate lunar landing sites, particularly near the Moon's south pole. It brings site selection, time-dependent Sun and Earth visibility, and illustrative lunar relay coverage into a single, accessible interface. The project responds to a central problem in lunar mission planning: a site suitable for science may be difficult to illuminate or contact from Earth, and changing a launch date may substantially change those conditions. ShackleComm makes these trade-offs visible so that students, educators, researchers, and interested members of the public can rapidly compare scenarios.
details:
ShackleComm

1. The mission

The mission assigned to our team was to develop software that makes selecting landing locations and dates for lunar missions easier. These decisions involve several interdependent factors, particularly illumination, communications and the surrounding terrain. Temperature and scientific accessibility are also relevant to real mission design, although ShackleComm does not numerically predict temperature or certify landing safety.

Although specialized software for these tasks already exists, some tools can be difficult for non-specialists to operate and cumbersome for quick comparisons. Our goal was therefore not only to analyze potential lunar landing sites and dates, but also to present the results in an intuitive way for students, educators, researchers and the general public. We also wanted the application to remain extensible as more authoritative lunar mapping and communications data become available.

Since the beginning of human exploration, the desire to reach beyond Earth has been a powerful motivation. Between 1969 and 1972, twelve astronauts from six Apollo missions walked on the Moon, all at near-side landing sites. More than fifty years later, the Artemis program is preparing a return to the lunar surface with a different geographic focus: the lunar south pole. The challenge is not a shortage of scientific information; it is making complex, time-dependent information accessible enough for rapid exploration and comparison.

ShackleComm responds to the NASA Space Apps Challenge Lunar Landing Site Navigator brief by combining site selection, adjustable dates, Sun and Earth visibility, estimated solar irradiance, and direct or relayed communication opportunities in one visual application.

1.1 The structure of the Moon

Like Earth, the Moon is a differentiated rocky body with a crust, mantle and core. Its core is comparatively small, with an iron-rich inner region, a surrounding liquid layer and a partially molten boundary zone. The mantle is composed mainly of silicate minerals such as olivine and pyroxene. Its crust varies in thickness and composition between the near and far sides, a distinction studied by missions including GRAIL. Above the crust lies the regolith: fragmented rock and dust created by billions of years of impacts.

The lunar surface has two broad geological domains. The brighter highlands (terrae) largely preserve the ancient, cratered crust. The darker maria are impact basins filled by volcanic basalt, often forming relatively smooth plains. The preservation of craters is exceptional because the Moon lacks Earth's atmosphere, liquid-water erosion and active plate tectonics.

This geological variation matters for landing-site selection. A low-lying basalt plain may be easier to approach than a mountainous crater rim, but an elevated polar ridge may offer advantages in sunlight or communication geometry. The best scientific target and the most accessible operational location are not always the same.

1.2 The Apollo zone and early landing criteria

Apollo landing sites were shaped by the technology and safety requirements of the 1960s. The missions targeted accessible locations on the Earth-facing lunar hemisphere, where direct communication was possible without lunar relay satellites. Early planning emphasized equatorial and relatively flat regions, although the precise acceptable landing area and trajectory constraints varied by mission rather than constituting a single permanent geographic boundary.

Selection criteria included terrain smoothness, low slopes, limited boulders and craters, unobstructed approach paths, communications visibility, propellant margins, launch-window flexibility and the ability to use suitable return trajectories.

Apollo 11 landed on 20 July 1969, when Eagle touched down in Mare Tranquillitatis with Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin. Later missions progressively emphasized scientific diversity. Apollo 12 returned to a mare region; Apollo 14 investigated the Fra Mauro formation; Apollo 15 explored Hadley–Apennine; Apollo 16 reached the Descartes highlands; and Apollo 17 investigated Taurus–Littrow. Together, these missions sampled environments from volcanic plains to ancient crustal highlands.

Figure 1. Mare Tranquillitatis and the Apollo 11 region. The source document attributes the underlying lunar topographic illustration to NASA/LROC; elevations and colors are illustrative of the published map.

1.3 Artemis and the lunar south pole

The Artemis program shifts attention toward the Moon's south polar region. In August 2022, NASA identified thirteen candidate regions, including Peak Near Shackleton, Connecting Ridge, de Gerlache, Haworth, Malapert Massif and Nobile Rim. In October 2024, NASA published nine updated candidate regions for further study: Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2 and Slater Plain. These represent regions containing many potential landing sites, not nine pre-approved touchdown coordinates. NASA 2022 · NASA 2024

The criteria have broadened considerably since Apollo. Teams now examine scientific value, terrain and slope, illumination, communication access, launch opportunities and the capability of the transport and landing systems. A site-date combination must work as an integrated mission scenario.

NASA's updated program plan assigns Artemis III to a low-Earth-orbit lander-operations demonstration in 2027, with Artemis IV targeted for the first crewed Artemis landing near the lunar south pole in 2028. These are plans, not guarantees of future launch dates. NASA Artemis III · NASA Artemis IV

1.4 Topographic differences between lunar regions

The lunar terrain can be grouped into several operationally distinct environments:

  • Equatorial maria: Broad basaltic plains, generally smoother than heavily cratered highlands, with scattered impact craters and local obstacles. Near the equator, lunar days and nights last approximately 14 Earth days each; this is the familiar Apollo landing environment.
  • Highlands (terrae): Ancient anorthositic crust with dense cratering, slopes and uneven relief. Landing and traverse operations are more complex, and lighting depends strongly on terrain and latitude.
  • Impact basins and mountain rings: Deep basins, concentric mountain systems, escarpments and rilles. These offer high scientific value but complex landing approaches and local visibility conditions.
  • Far side: Predominantly highland terrain with relatively few maria, including the South Pole–Aitken Basin. The lunar body generally blocks direct-to-Earth surface communication, making relays necessary at many sites.
  • South-polar permanently shadowed regions (PSRs): Deep craters that can remain unilluminated over extremely long periods. Their low temperatures may preserve volatiles but present severe power, thermal and accessibility challenges.
  • South-polar peaks and crater rims: Elevated massifs and ridges between steep crater walls and shadowed depressions. Some offer extended illumination windows, but visibility and terrain can vary substantially over short distances.

1.5 Why the south pole is scientifically attractive

At first sight, the south pole may appear unsuitable for landing: its terrain is rugged, much of it lies in deep shadow, and the Sun remains close to the horizon. Nevertheless, several factors make it important for future exploration.

Water ice and permanently shadowed regions. The lunar spin axis is tilted only about 1.5° relative to the ecliptic. Near the poles, the Sun stays low, allowing some deep crater interiors to remain permanently shadowed. Measurements by missions such as Lunar Prospector, Chandrayaan-1, LCROSS and the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter have provided evidence for polar hydrogen and water-bearing material. Accessible ice could eventually support life-support systems and in-situ resource utilization.

Potentially extended solar illumination. Elevated crater rims and ridges can rise above nearby shadowed terrain and receive sunlight for long intervals. These are not universally or continuously illuminated; the exact result depends on the site, terrain horizon and date. Solar-power planning therefore requires an analysis of each location and mission window.

Thermal environment. Temperature differences between illuminated and shadowed surfaces can be extreme. Permanently shadowed crater floors may become exceptionally cold, while illuminated regolith warms. Thermal suitability is significant to real missions, but it remains a future capability rather than an output of ShackleComm.

Communications and scientific value. Earth may appear very low on the horizon as seen from a polar location, and the Moon's libration can change whether it is visible. Some sites have favorable direct communication geometry; others benefit from relay satellites. Meanwhile, polar ice deposits and ancient geological formations are valuable scientific records.

Taken together, these factors explain why a quick visual assessment of lighting and communications can be useful before any detailed engineering evaluation.

2. Telecommunications

Telecommunications are fundamental to space exploration. They allow spacecraft and surface installations to send scientific data, report system status and receive commands from mission-control teams on Earth. A base with adequate lighting but no available communication route may still be unsuitable for an intended mission schedule.

2.1 Direct communications between Earth and the Moon

NASA's Deep Space Network (DSN) is a global system of radio-antenna complexes managed through the Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Its three principal complexes are located at Goldstone (United States), Madrid / Robledo de Chavela (Spain) and Canberra / Tidbinbilla (Australia). Their geographic separation helps support contacts with deep-space missions as Earth rotates. NASA DSN

Figure 2. The three original NASA-attributed DSN antenna photographs, displayed separately in their original reading order. They illustrate the network discussed above; the source PDF does not identify which station appears in each photograph.

However, the existence of the network does not guarantee that every lunar location can contact Earth at every moment. The local lunar horizon, Earth–Moon orientation, and visibility of the Moon from a particular Earth station all matter.

ShackleComm therefore analyzes three Earth-fixed ground-station locations rather than treating Earth as a single abstract point:

  • Madrid, Spain: 40.42917° N, 4.24972° W.
  • Goldstone, USA: 35.28139° N, 116.77889° W.
  • Canberra, Australia: 35.40167° S, 148.98222° E.

The coordinates above are the reference values used in the application's model. They represent the station complexes approximately, not every individual DSN antenna or its exact surveyed position.

2.2 Application of direct communications in ShackleComm

Users select a lunar location and a UTC simulation date. The application estimates Earth's local azimuth and elevation above the selected site's horizon, then checks whether each DSN complex can geometrically see the Moon. The station locations rotate with Earth and remain fixed on its surface.

The method follows the principle used in higher-fidelity astronomical analysis: compute the apparent direction to Earth or a spacecraft, compare it with the local horizon, and determine whether the unobstructed path exists. JPL Horizons is an external reference for verification; ShackleComm does not query Horizons live and does not claim to reproduce its full precision.

For a direct lunar-base-to-station connection, both of the following must hold:

  1. Earth is above the modeled lunar terrain horizon in the relevant azimuth.
  2. The Moon is above the station's ideal geometric horizon at the selected time.

This constitutes geometric direct-to-Earth (DTE) availability, not a guaranteed radio session. Actual antenna availability, weather, radio power, link budgets, Earth-station terrain and operating schedules are outside the current model.

2.3 Communications through lunar relay satellites

When the lunar base cannot directly see a DSN complex, a relay spacecraft may provide an alternative. A relay is useful only if the complete path is clear: the lunar site must see the satellite, and that satellite must have an unobstructed line to at least one Earth station.

Figure 3. Simplified direct and relay communication routes. A satellite being overhead does not necessarily mean it is connected to Earth.

The main Earth Connection indicator combines both routes. A direct route is recorded as DTE, a complete satellite-assisted route as relay coverage, and the combined availability is their logical union. The coverage statistics avoid double-counting an interval in which both routes are available.

2.4 NASA LCRNS reference constellation

The application includes five proposed NASA LCRNS Reference Constellation 3.1 vehicles, labelled LCRNS-1 through LCRNS-5 in the interface and SV-1 through SV-5 in the underlying source data. The reference design is documented by NASA Goddard and intended to support analysis of lunar south-polar communications and navigation. It is not a list of five launched or currently tracked NASA satellites. The final operational constellation design and service implementation may differ. NASA LCRNS Reference Constellation 3.1

  1. SV-1 / LCRNS-1: Semi-major axis: 11,315.94 km; eccentricity: 0.691982; inclination: 59.37°.
  2. SV-2 / LCRNS-2: Semi-major axis: 11,317.95 km; eccentricity: 0.691982; inclination: 58.95°.
  3. SV-3 / LCRNS-3: Semi-major axis: 11,305.41 km; eccentricity: 0.691982; inclination: 52.73°.
  4. SV-4 / LCRNS-4: Semi-major axis: 11,326.30 km; eccentricity: 0.691982; inclination: 52.51°.
  5. SV-5 / LCRNS-5: Semi-major axis: 11,307.88 km; eccentricity: 0.691982; inclination: 56.31°.

These are the published Table 1 orbital-element values, shown for context. The code initializes propagation from NASA's Table 2 Moon-centered ICRF position and velocity vectors at 1 March 2027, 00:00 UTC. The Table 1 angular elements belong to a different lunar reference frame and are not substituted into the ICRF propagation.

2.5 Future-mission scenarios

One objective of the project is to explore how changes in mission dates might affect illumination and communication opportunities. The current date selector supports 1 January 2020 through 31 December 2035; it does not offer 2050 as a selectable date. Even within that range, distant predictions of relay location are illustrative because the code uses simplified orbital dynamics, and the reference spacecraft might never be deployed in the assumed configuration.

The system therefore distinguishes published reference state data, calculated geometric predictions, and model assumptions. This distinction is essential when using future scenarios in education or early-stage mission studies.

3. Our work

3.1 Our creative process

Friday. When we arrived on Friday, not all team members were able to attend. Rather than starting as a single group, we came from two smaller groups and an additional individual participant, while two colleagues were absent. After the presentation, we came together to select a project. Our first difficulty was that the groups had initially preferred different challenges; we therefore began by discussing which direction offered the strongest common objective.

Saturday. With the full team assembled, we reviewed the proposed challenges one by one. We considered the other teams, existing solutions, technical feasibility and the skills available within our group. By approximately 10:40, we had chosen Lunar Landing Site Navigator and immediately began investigating orbital mechanics, telecommunications and prototype approaches. By 16:00, different team members had advanced several competing prototypes. We had to select a common foundation and resolve design disagreements before converging on the application we ultimately presented.

Sunday. We concentrated on the presentation and the final details of the application. We tested the simulator, replaced illustrative orbital placeholders with published NASA reference-state information where available, refined the user interface and consolidated the research into project documentation. The work also involved checking which scientific inputs were genuine source data and which remained approximations in our prototype.

3.2 The product: overview

ShackleComm is a browser-based web application with a three-dimensional visualization of the Earth–Moon environment and the five proposed NASA LCRNS Reference Constellation 3.1 spacecraft. It estimates solar illumination, horizontal solar irradiance and potential direct or relayed communications with NASA DSN ground-station locations. Users can examine known lunar sites, select custom coordinates, compare multiple locations and inspect results for adjustable time windows.

The emphasis is accessibility: technical data are available, but the interface prioritizes immediate visual understanding. The welcome screen introduces the project; the principal screen uses minimal retractable panels, identifiable colors, interactive orbital controls and concise status indicators.

Current capabilities:

  • Site selection: 13 curated lunar locations, plus arbitrary coordinates entered manually or selected on the 3D or 2D map.
  • Recommendations: South-polar candidates ranked by their relative Viability score for the selected period.
  • Viability: A 0–100 relative index, shown with a red–ochre–green gradient; 55% sunlight availability plus 45% combined Earth communication availability.
  • Comparison: Pin and compare up to three selected locations; pin controls appear contextually.
  • Visualization: Interactive 3D Earth–Moon scene, 2D south-pole view and 2D global lunar map, with satellite labels and optional orbital and communication lines.
  • Orbital display: Approximate Moon-around-Earth guide and an illustrative Earth–Moon-barycenter orbit around the Sun. The scene does not display all distances at one physical scale.
  • Time: Start date from 2020–2035; 7-day, 14-day or approximately 29.53-day windows; daily stepping, time scrubber and variable-speed playback.
  • Illumination: Local solar elevation, modeled horizon obstruction, sunlit/shadowed condition, estimated horizontal solar flux, transition timing and window averages.
  • Communication: Individual geometric checks for Madrid, Goldstone and Canberra; visible and linked LCRNS satellites; direct, relay and combined Earth availability.
  • Telemetry: Expandable live and time-window statistics, local horizon plot and communication timeline.
  • User interface: Branded welcome screen, responsive layouts, retractable sidebars, contextual actions and a methodology/help panel.

Figure 4. Original page-15 application interface and principal controls. The screenshot records one stage of the project; the live interface may have minor styling or layout changes.

3.3 Design architecture

The application uses a functional, data-driven calculation layer coordinated by a central mutable state object. Orbital and visibility functions operate on structured datasets; rendering and interaction functions transform their outputs into the user interface. This is more precise than describing the entire program as purely functional programming, because the browser UI, state and Three.js scene necessarily contain mutable objects.

The orbital datasets are stored as configuration data, allowing the same calculation to be applied to all five reference spacecraft. Important functions include getEphemeris(), getReferenceTwoBodyOrbit(), propagateRelaySatellite(), computeHorizonProfile(), getRelayVisibilityAtSite(), getDsnVisibility(), getRelayDsnLinks() and analyzeTimeframe(). rebuildActiveWindow(), updateInstantaneousTelemetry() and animationLoop() connect the calculations to the presentation.

Figure 5. Original ShackleComm architecture diagram from the source PDF, showing the central state, physics calculations, time-window analysis, live sampling and visualization outputs.

The following complementary diagram expands the same structure into the application's current data flow:

Figure 6. Current application architecture. The live sample is evaluated for the exact simulated timestamp, while summary percentages are estimated from finite time samples.

The main analysis window uses 120 intervals for the active location (with 121 sample points, including the endpoint). Lower-resolution 72-interval results may be cached for location recommendations and pinned-site comparisons. Playback time progresses continuously, although the 3D rendering budget is throttled to approximately 30 updates per second to manage GPU and DOM costs. This is a rendering target, not a guaranteed measured frame rate.

The web implementation uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, Three.js/WebGL and Canvas 2D. It is client-side: there is no required account system, project database or backend service. The HTML includes embedded branding and uses external dependencies and optional image textures, with lightweight procedural rendering fallbacks. The satellite models currently drawn in the scene are low-cost geometric primitives, not verified models of actual LCRNS flight hardware.

3.4 Engineering trade-offs

During development, we made several choices to reach a usable prototype within the challenge's time constraints.

Website rather than downloadable application. A browser-based interface was easier to distribute for educational use. It also encouraged a lightweight design: very large terrain meshes and high-resolution elevation datasets were not integrated into the final prototype.

Fast terrain approximation rather than full LOLA ingestion. We originally wanted detailed lunar topographic profiles. The shipped version instead constructs a synthetic elevation surface and samples it to estimate a local horizon. This supports interactive exploration, but its shadows and site rankings should not be represented as NASA-measured local conditions.

Reference constellation rather than a freely configurable network. The application models the five NASA LCRNS reference spacecraft. A generic feature for inserting arbitrary additional relay satellites was deferred; such an extension would need clear provenance and separate assumptions.

Lighting and communications rather than thermal prediction. Temperature prediction was considered but not implemented. The final prototype concentrates on interpreting solar illumination and communication visibility, which are already substantial and interdependent challenges.

Performance rather than spacecraft-model detail. The scene uses inexpensive satellite markers and camera-facing labels. An external decorative spacecraft model was considered, but not adopted as a required asset without hardware-specific performance validation. Preserving responsiveness and avoiding unnecessary loading dependencies took priority.

3.5 Interface explanation and workflow

The primary interface includes a view selector, date controls, playback controls, a location explorer, a telemetry sidebar and a bottom status rail. Users begin at the branded introduction screen, select Start, choose a lunar site, and then explore the consequences of changing the date or location.

To compare locations, a user selects a site, pins it, and repeats this for up to two additional sites. The selected location is highlighted on the Moon and in the site list. The panels can be retracted, and more detailed telemetry can be expanded only when needed. A red–ochre–green Viability label provides an immediate visual summary; its numerical meaning is explicitly defined in the next section.

4. Scientific methodology and implementation

This section expands the original proposed methodology to describe what the current code actually calculates, which source data are used, and which quantities remain approximate. It corresponds to the methodology information available through the application's help panel.

4.1 Coordinates, time and approximate ephemerides

The simulator uses lunar latitude and longitude for a selected surface point and UTC for the analysis time. Analytical periods are used to approximate lunar phase, subsolar longitude and latitude, Earth libration and Moon orbital orientation. The implementation includes the Moon's approximately 27.32-day sidereal and 29.53-day synodic cycles, with simplified optical libration terms reaching approximately ±7.6° longitude and ±6.68° latitude.

These formulas are appropriate for a lightweight visual demonstration, but they are not interchangeable with JPL's high-precision ephemerides. In particular, selecting a time does not initiate a live Horizons query. For scientific verification, the relevant azimuth/elevation estimates should be independently compared with JPL Horizons and its manual.

The 3D scene displays the Moon in an approximate geocentric ecliptic coordinate frame. The lunar reference body rotates relative to this frame, but the LCRNS spacecraft orbital planes are propagated in an inertial reference frame rather than being rigidly attached to the Moon's rotating surface.

4.2 Local horizon and line-of-sight geometry

For an observer at lunar latitude ϕo​ and longitude  λo​, and a distant target with apparent subpoint (ϕt,λt)(ϕt​,λt​), the simplified spherical relation for target elevation is:

The application also derives the target azimuth and compares its elevation hh with an azimuth-dependent terrain-horizon threshold H(A)H(A). Visible means that the target exceeds that modeled threshold.

The horizon model is built by computeHorizonProfile(): it samples 72 azimuth sectors at 5° spacing and checks nearby terrain points at selected distances, including a lunar-curvature correction using a mean lunar radius of 1,737.4 km. The altitude function getElevationKm() is procedural and includes idealized local features near major reference sites. It is not an imported LOLA digital elevation model. Thus, the method is geometric, but the present horizon values are approximations.

Figure 7. Example NASA lunar Earth-visibility visualization included in the original documentation. This is an external scientific illustration, not a map generated from ShackleComm's synthetic horizon model.

4.3 Illumination and horizontal solar irradiance

Once the Sun's elevation h⊙​ and modeled horizon are known, a site is counted as illuminated if the Sun clears its local terrain-horizon threshold. The displayed solar irradiance on an ideal horizontal surface is approximated by:

The value 1,361 W/m² represents the approximate mean direct solar irradiance normal to sunlight at 1 astronomical unit. The Moon has essentially no atmosphere, so there is no modeled atmospheric diffuse illumination. This formula describes a horizontal receiving surface, not a sun-tracking panel, photovoltaic electrical output, thermal balance or illumination of inclined local slopes. The code does not apply time-varying Sun–Moon distance, finite solar-disk partial shadows or measured 3D terrain shadow maps.

4.4 Direct DSN visibility

For each DSN complex, getEarthDsnGeometry() and getDsnVisibility() estimate the Moon's Earth-side direction using an approximate lunar-position formula and Greenwich mean sidereal time. The program tests the elevation of the Moon above the station's ideal horizon and combines this with Earth visibility from the lunar site.

The direct availability condition can be summarized as:

This is a geometric visibility check. Ground-station mountain horizons, operational scheduling, antenna constraints, radio frequency effects and weather are not included.

4.5 NASA LCRNS two-body propagation

For each proposed reference spacecraft, the application uses NASA's published Moon-centered ICRF Cartesian position r0r0​ in kilometres and velocity v0​ in kilometres per second at 2027-03-01 00:00 UTC. The code derives a Keplerian two-body ellipse from these states using lunar gravitational parameter μ=4902.800066  km3 s−2μ=4902.800066km3s−2.

The semi-major axis follows the vis-viva relation:

At a later time, the mean anomaly is advanced by M(t)=M0+nΔt, Kepler's equation M=E−e * sin⁡E is solved iteratively, and the satellite position is reconstructed in the original inertial orbital plane. The relevant vector is then transformed into the rotating lunar local frame for surface-horizon tests.

The resulting reference ellipses have periods close to 30 hours. However, the simulation omits the high-degree lunar gravity field, detailed third-body forces and radiation-pressure effects required for operational orbit determination. NASA's LCRNS publication calls for a higher-fidelity propagation approach; therefore, positions away from the published epoch are illustrative two-body predictions, not NASA-validated future states.

4.6 Full satellite-to-DSN link validation

For every reference spacecraft, getRelayVisibilityAtSite() checks whether its apparent elevation exceeds both the modeled local terrain horizon and an assumed 5° lunar-terminal minimum elevation. This 5° mask is an application assumption, not an orbital requirement copied from NASA's LCRNS constellation paper.

getRelayDsnLinks() then tests the spacecraft's straight-line path to each Earth-fixed DSN complex. The geometric model uses physical-kilometre coordinates, a spherical-Earth horizon test and obstruction tests against the Moon. A satellite counts as Linked only when it is visible from the lunar base and has a clear line to at least one Earth station.

This distinction explains why a satellite may be Overhead but not Linked: the base-to-satellite hop may be available even when the satellite-to-DSN hop is not.

4.7 Time-window coverage and Viability

analyzeTimeframe() evaluates the state of the selected lunar location over a chosen 7-day, 14-day or approximately 29.53-day period. The active window is estimated using 120 equal intervals. The program counts the intervals in which the site is illuminated, a direct DSN connection exists, a full relay connection exists and either communication route exists.

For example, estimated communication availability is:

The displayed Viability index is a relative comparison aid:

The score ranges from 0 to 100 and uses a continuous red–ochre–green color gradient. It reflects only the two weighted factors above; it does not incorporate actual hazard probability, engineering slope limits, thermal acceptability, science value, spacecraft mass, reliability or lander capabilities. Consequently, a higher Viability score does not constitute a certification that a site is safe or that a mission will succeed.

Sampled coverage percentages and transition times have finite temporal resolution. Instantaneous live readouts are evaluated at the current simulated timestamp, while the time-window summary is a numerical approximation rather than a continuous-time proof of coverage.

4.8 Orbital visualization and rendering scale

The 3D lunar-orbit guide uses a mean Moon orbital radius of approximately 384,400 km, an eccentricity near 0.0549 and inclination near 5.145°. The Earth–Sun illustration draws an approximate Earth–Moon barycenter orbit, based on JPL's mean J2000 ecliptic elements and secular rates: a≈1.00000261 AU≈1.00000261AU, e≈0.01671123 at J2000. Kepler's equation is used to draw the ellipse and position the reference body along it. JPL approximate planetary positions

The 3D scene is deliberately not to uniform physical scale. Earth–Moon separation and the Earth–Sun orbit are compressed or enlarged for visibility. The solar orbital guide is educational and is not used to determine the application's lunar communication or sunlight percentages. Likewise, displayed satellite size is illustrative; physical-kilometre geometry is used for the intended link-obstruction calculations.

4.9 Scientific verification and extension roadmap

A future, mission-grade version should replace or validate the following components with traceable datasets and numerical uncertainty estimates:

  • Topography: Load actual LOLA or combined lunar digital elevation grids; compute site-specific horizon masks and finite-solar-disk shadowing.
  • Ephemerides: Compare Sun/Earth azimuth and elevation with JPL Horizons across the date range and carefully manage time scales and reference frames.
  • Relay propagation: Integrate the NASA-described gravity and perturbation model, or import authoritative spacecraft ephemeris files when available.
  • Communications: Add realistic ground-station local horizons, antenna pointing limits, mission scheduling, link budgets and terminal capabilities.
  • Power and safety: Model panel orientation, efficiencies, battery storage, thermal environment, local slope, hazards and landing-system requirements.

Until those extensions are implemented and verified, ShackleComm should be presented as a transparent educational prototype with source-grounded initial satellite states.

5. Engineering trade-offs and limitations

The main trade-off throughout development has been balancing three goals: clarity, scientific traceability and browser performance. The application deliberately favors quick interaction over processing heavy global terrain grids or full numerical orbit integrations. As a result, its strengths and limitations should be considered together.

  • Site catalog
    • Implemented: Named historical and south-polar coordinates.
    • Limitation: The list is curated; some names are project or historical references rather than current NASA-approved touchdown coordinates.
    • Implemented: Procedural elevation features and a 72-sector directional horizon.
    • Limitation: No measured LOLA digital elevation model is loaded; local shadows and derived site scores are approximate.
    • Implemented: Analytical, low-precision ephemerides including lunar libration terms.
    • Limitation: These do not provide JPL Horizons-level accuracy.
    • Implemented: Geometric illumination and direct irradiance on a horizontal surface.
    • Limitation: No photovoltaic energy, thermal or tilted-surface incidence model.
    • Implemented: Three fixed geographic complexes and geometric visibility checks.
    • Limitation: No antenna-specific operations, weather, local Earth-station terrain or link budgets.
    • Implemented: Five proposed NASA initial states with inertial two-body orbital previews.
    • Limitation: These are not a launched constellation or a full perturbation-model propagation.
    • Implemented: 3D and 2D views, comparison, orbital guides and telemetry.
    • Limitation: Non-uniform display scaling; performance varies by browser and device.
    • Implemented: Selectable time windows from 2020–2035.
    • Limitation: Long-term orbital predictions remain model-dependent.

Our principal contribution is therefore not a claim to replace NASA's scientific systems. It is a compact interpretation layer that allows users to see why time, geography, illumination and communication must be considered together when studying lunar landing options.

ShackleComm — By endurance we conquer.
